analysis.one_liner: Bans stock, crypto, and commodity trading by the president, members of Congress, justices, and Fed officials.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors on September 18, 2025, has sat in the Senate Homeland Security Committee with no hearing or vote ever scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the president, vice president, members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, and top Federal Reserve officials — along with their spouses and young dependent children — from owning or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, and crypto. They would have to sell such holdings within 120 days, and blind trusts would no longer work as a hiding place if the official benefits from the trust's assets. Knowing violators would face fines of at least 10% of the asset's value.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, who would be governed by officials with no personal financial stake in the companies their laws and regulatory decisions move. Covered officials would also gain a bright-line rule that shields them from conflict-of-interest accusations.

how_it_helps.text: Bans holding, buying, or selling individual stocks, futures, commodities, and crypto by members of Congress, the president, vice president, Supreme Court justices, and senior Federal Reserve officials, and covers their spouses and dependent children.
Requires divestiture within 120 days and ends the use of blind trusts as a shield whenever the official is a beneficial owner of the trust's assets.

Imposes a fine of at least 10% of the value of any asset held or traded in violation, and requires ethics offices to publish online every request to extend the divestiture deadline and the decision on it.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the president and vice president, Supreme Court justices, senior Federal Reserve officials, and their spouses and dependent children, who would have to sell individual stocks, crypto, and similar assets within 120 days; the ethics offices supervising them would take on new administrative work.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is a civil fine set by the same ethics offices that supervise the official, applies only to 'knowing' violations, and at 10% of an asset's value could be smaller than the profit from a well-timed trade.
The ban only reaches dependent children under age 19, leaving adult children and other relatives available as legal holding places for a covered official's assets.
A total ban could discourage experienced private-sector candidates from seeking office, since they would have to divest within 120 days of taking their seat.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the clearest conflict of interest in government: officials writing rules and policies that move companies they personally own. Its design is imperfect — no criminal penalty, a knowledge requirement, fines that may not outweigh the gains from a violation, and a dependent-child definition that stops at age 19 — but the core prohibition is simple and would be hard to circumvent through trusts. The larger obstacle is political rather than substantive: with zero cosponsors and no committee action, it has not moved at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the No Stock Act on September 18, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No hearing, markup, or vote has taken place since the referral, and no other senator has signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered officials, who so far keep the right to hold and trade individual stocks, crypto, and other assets the bill would strip from them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials who keep their trading rights

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the No Stock Act and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Rand Paul, R-KY)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the September 18, 2025 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the bill has zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split has formed in the record yet.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and other covered senior officials (and their families)
industries.note: They would have to sell individual stocks, futures, commodities, and crypto within 120 days, keeping only diversified funds, Treasuries, and similar holdings, with fines of at least 10% of an asset's value for knowing violations. Their financial interest in keeping these trading rights runs directly against the public's interest in conflict-free government.

The ban would strip a small class of wealthy buyers — covered officials — from trading crypto, meme coins, tokens, and NFTs, but the bill explicitly carves out payment stablecoins as defined by the GENIUS Act, sparing that sector.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to ban stock trading by members of Congress have repeatedly died in committee in recent Congresses, even with cosponsors. With none, no committee action, and roughly 15 months left in the session, this bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
